content: At the time of randomization, the rate of postnatal HIV transmission was extremely low and showed no significant difference between infants who received extended nevirapine (NVP) prophylaxis and those who received a placebo. In a large European cohort of high-risk mother-infant pairs, no differences in serious adverse events were observed among infants who received one, two, or three antiretroviral drugs. When comparing the incidence of neutropenia between the two-drug and three-drug regimens, there was a trend toward more events in the three-drug group, but this difference was not statistically significant. A single-arm study conducted in Thailand on non-breastfeeding infants born to mothers who received less than eight weeks of antepartum antiretroviral therapy (ART) provided intensified infant prophylaxis with zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), and NVP for two weeks, followed by AZT and 3TC for an additional two weeks. No intrapartum infections were observed, and the rate of serious adverse events among infants receiving this intensified prophylaxis was lower than in a historical observational cohort. None of the reviewed studies specifically addressed infants identified as HIV-exposed during the postpartum period or those exposed to an incident maternal HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding. However, the findings from the systematic review may be applicable to these scenarios. Recommendations for extended prophylaxis in breastfeeding infants are based on the assumption that maternal ART is initiated at or before the start of infant prophylaxis, as the purpose of infant prophylaxis is to provide temporary protection while maternal viral load decreases on ART. The 2016 WHO consolidated HIV guidelines highlight various factors to consider when assessing the risk of HIV transmission in infants. Factors such as prolonged rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, and low birth weight are no longer associated with increased transmission risk when mothers are on ART. The primary determinants of transmission risk in the ART era are maternal viral load and the duration of maternal ART. If viral load testing is unavailable, priority should be given to obtaining and processing viral load specimens for pregnant and breastfeeding women. The 2021 WHO clinical guidelines recommend that all pregnant women, regardless of when ART was initiated, undergo viral load testing at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at delivery if testing was not done earlier). This is to identify women at risk of treatment failure and/or those who may deliver infants at higher risk of perinatal transmission. High-risk infants are defined as those born to mothers with established HIV infection who received less than four weeks of ART before delivery, mothers with a viral load >1,000 copies/mL within four weeks of delivery, mothers with incident HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or mothers newly identified as HIV-positive postpartum. Providing multiple drugs to newborns poses operational challenges. While AZT and NVP are recommended based on available data, their differing dosing schedules (once daily for NVP and twice daily for AZT) complicate administration. Provider training and innovative dosing strategies, such as twice-daily NVP dosing, may simplify implementation. When the recommended regimen is unavailable, alternative options like raltegravir (RAL), 3TC, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), or fixed-dose combinations containing AZT, NVP, and 3TC may be considered. Consistent with early infant diagnosis recommendations, no specific testing approach is recommended for high-risk newborns. However, birth diagnostic nucleic acid testing (NAT) may be considered. Infants identified as HIV-exposed postpartum have a high cumulative risk of already having acquired HIV by the time prophylaxis is initiated, and an HIV NAT test should be performed at the time of initiating prophylaxis. In cases where maternal viral suppression cannot be ensured throughout breastfeeding, such as when mothers refuse or are unable to start or continue ART, are poorly adherent, or have elevated viral loads when infant prophylaxis is about to end, infant prophylaxis may serve as a backup solution to prevent postnatal HIV transmission. National guidelines could consider allowing clinical providers the option to extend infant prophylaxis beyond the recommended 6or 12-week period in clearly defined scenarios. Research gaps include the need for clinical and pharmacological studies to develop improved antiretroviral drug formulations for newborns and infants, including fixed-dose combinations. Studies on alternative drugs for prophylaxis, such as integrase inhibitors, which may be better tolerated and more effective, are also needed. Additionally, research is required to evaluate the clinical relevance of postnatal viremic episodes in breastfeeding mothers and their contribution to infant HIV infection, as well as the potential added benefit of enhanced prophylaxis in populations with effective maternal ART programs but known adherence challenges. Implementation science research should focus on defining high-risk infants in the context of universal maternal ART and evaluating service delivery models to improve adherence to enhanced postnatal prophylaxis and retention in care. Improving service delivery and implementing a comprehensive postnatal care package for HIV-exposed infants is critical. Barriers to effective infant HIV services include socioeconomic and traditional factors that influence mother-infant pair retention. Programs should integrate effective interventions into service packages, emphasizing community engagement to support uptake. Proven interventions include client-focused strategies like reminder text messaging, conditional cash incentives, and male partner involvement, as well as health system-focused measures like point-of-care testing, provider training, enhanced counseling, and peer support. Promoting integration within maternal, neonatal, and child health services can reduce care fragmentation and ensure infants remain in the testing cascade until final diagnosis. Strong antenatal and well-baby care systems provide opportunities to strengthen service delivery for HIV-exposed infants. Community engagement and community-based services play a vital role in supporting HIV-exposed infant care, including community-based HIV testing and active follow-up of mother-infant pairs. These interventions have been shown to reduce loss to follow-up and improve outcomes for both mothers and infants.
